title: B-flat cornets and low pitch for dance halls
summary: Laine says all cornets were B-flat except Johnny Provanzano's Italian E-flat, and that bands used low pitch indoors and high pitch on the street.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: Did they play regular cornets in those days or were they different?
In those days when you started out. The cornet, was it a B-flat cornet?

Yes, all B-flats. All B-flats. Only one E-flat. That was Johnny Provanzana. That's one man, E-flat. One man, Johnny Provanzana played in E-flat. It came directly from Italy. I see. Had side keys on it. The funniest looking thing ever you've seen in your life. E-flat cornet. All the rest and paid these fats. And most of our music we played in a ball or a dance but all in low pitch. All in low pitch. Without on the street. Terrorist. High pitch.
Why was that? Why was that? Did you hear it farther? Yes.
You don't need that in the hall.

No, no. No, no. You wouldn't need that in the hall. See? That's why we'd play all low pitch in the hall. See? And we used to get the value of music in the hall better than you would on the street. Yeah.
Yeah. You mean by low pitch what key it was in or whether it was loud or soft?

No, no. What key would be in no matter what key would be in. What key would play in low pitch? Oh, yes. Oh, yes. We'd try first right on down low pitch. Why? You have no idea. We played many waltzes. It's written in waltz time. We played it in watch time.
